A holistic care system is debated as a vital framework connecting childcare, eldercare, disability support, and healthcare to support inclusive growth and Viksit Bharat 2047.

Proposals to address this include establishing a National Caregiving Council, a National Care Economy Mission, and formalizing the undervalued care workforce.
Recognising care as an essential economic investment rather than simple welfare expenditure will strengthen female labour participation and support an ageing population.
sum.text:
India’s development strategy has prioritised highways, metro lines, electrification and digital platforms, but care remains an under-recognised foundation of growth. Without affordable services, families, especially women, bear unpaid work and lose economic opportunities. With an ageing population and rising demand for caregivers, India must connect childcare, eldercare, disability support and healthcare through an accessible, quality, adequately funded care system to advance inclusive development and Viksit Bharat 2047.
Holistic Care System: It is a broader framework that connects childcare, eldercare, disability support and healthcare to meet people’s care needs throughout life.
Holistic Healthcare: It is an approach that addresses a person’s physical, mental and social well-being through preventive, promotive, curative, rehabilitative and palliative care.
Relationship Between the Two: Holistic healthcare is one component of a holistic care system , which also includes wider caregiving services and support for families and caregivers.
Person-Centred Approach: Care should respond to individual needs and support people’s dignity, well-being and participation through accessible and quality services.
Women’s Employment Opportunities: Affordable childcare can reduce caregiving barriers and allow more women to pursue employment, leisure and participation in public life.
Unpaid Care Burden: The Time Use Survey 2024 found that 41% of women aged 15–59 provided unpaid care, averaging 140 minutes daily .
Women’s Labour Force Participation: The Periodic Labour Force Survey 2025 found that 44.4% of women outside the labour force cited childcare and homemaking as their main reason for staying out.

Healthier Population: Preventive and community-based healthcare can help address chronic conditions…

explain.headline: Supreme Court Notice on Digital News Publishers Challenge to Data Protection Act
static: The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, governs the processing of digital personal data in India while recognizing the right of individuals to protect their data.
Section 44(3) of the DPDPA amends the Right to Information Act, 2005, substituting Section 8(1)(j) to alter exemptions related to personal information disclosure.
The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) is the nodal ministry responsible for formulating rules and overseeing the implementation of data protection laws in India.
Journalistic exemptions or carve-outs exist in international data privacy frameworks like the European Union's GDPR to protect public interest reporting and source confidentiality.
explain.what: The Supreme Court has issued notice on a petition by the Digital News Publishers Association challenging the constitutional validity of provisions in the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, for lacking a journalistic exemption.
explain.why_in_news: The Digital News Publishers Association filed a comprehensive 698-page petition in the Supreme Court challenging the Act ahead of its enforcement from May 2027.
explain.background: The DPDP Act, 2023 regulates digital personal data processing but faces sharp criticism from press bodies like DNPA and the Editors Guild for omitting protections for investigative journalism and source confidentiality.
significance: Highlights the vital legislative tension between individual data privacy rights and the freedom of the press in investigative reporting.
Examines whether mandatory consent provisions under data protection laws can impede anti-corruption disclosures and public accountability.
Addresses statutory modifications to the Right to Information Act and their impact on accessing information in the public interest.
prelims: The petitioning body is the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA).
The provisions of the Act under challenge take effect from May 2027.
The bench hearing the petition was headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant.

texts.x: Public functionaries must not use privacy to seek exemption from scrutiny

points: The Supreme Court issued notice on a petition by the Digital News Publishers Association challenging the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.
The petitioner argues that requiring journalist consent and allowing data erasure will close down newsrooms and act as pre-censorship.
The core issue is the absence of an explicit journalistic carve-out in the Act, unlike jurisdictions like the European Union and Britain.
Senior Advocate Madhavi Divan stated that seeking subject permission before reporting would allow subjects to destroy evidence and intimidate witnesses.
The petition notes that individuals can withdraw consent and demand data erasure anytime without any public-interest safeguards.
The law grants broad exemptions to the state and powers to block public information, while failing to protect the press.
The Act allows the government to order data handlers to furnish information, potentially compromising reporter-informant privileged communications.
The petition was filed on October 6 by DNPA, representing 21 mainstream news outlets including Network18 and NDTV.
A Supreme Court bench comprising CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, and Justice V Mohana heard the matter.
sum.text:
The Supreme Court has issued notice on a petition challenging the provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, filed by the Digital News Publishers Association.“This is the first comprehensive petition by ‘legacy media’. We are the traditional, conventional legacy media. This will change the whole concept of news.
If I am left to the mercy of the data principal on whether he or she will give consent, the concept of news will be gone... It will close down the newsroom. What’s the point if I have to ask for permission and consent?” said Senior Advocate Madhavi Divan, representing the digital wings of 21 mainstream news outlets, according to LiveLaw.
Others raised similar concerns before. When the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 were notified on November 15 last year, the DIGIPUB News India Foundation said the Act and the Rules “endanger source confidentiality, hinder public-interest investigations, obstruct anti-corruption disclosures”. DIGIPUB said it had earlier submitted formal objections to the removal of the journalistic carve-out from the DPDPA, 2023 and also highlighted that Section 44(3) substitutes Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act, thereby abolishing the public-interest override and making access to information even more restrictive. Even the Editors Guild of India warned that without an explicit exemption, journalism risks being treated as personal data processing that requires consent, “thereby chilling newsgathering and hindering accountability journalism”Now, 21 news publishers, including outlets owned by Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, have told the Supreme Court that India’s data protection law would “render investigative journalism a benign and neutered recorder of events”.
The petition, filed on October 6 by the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), calls the law’s provisions “pre-censorship which is anathema to any democracy worth its name”. Running to 698 pages, it asks the court to quash most of the contentious provisions, which take effect from May 2027. DNPA’s members include Ambani’s Network18, Adani’s NDTV, the Indian Express and Times Internet, part of the Times of India group. Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana heard the matter on Tuesday.
The CJI said that a balance has to be struck between the rights of the citizens and those of the media. The bench issued notice on the petition as well as the application for stay. Divan informed the bench…

explain.headline: Deemed ineligible: on the Supreme Court and SIR
static: The Supreme Court of India is the highest judicial forum and final court of appeal under the Constitution of India, established under Article 124.
Judicial review allows the Supreme Court to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders, striking them down if they violate fundamental rights.
Public Interest Litigation (PIL) enables any public-spirited individual or group to approach the court for the protection of fundamental rights of marginalized or vulnerable sections.

points: The Election Commission of India filed an affidavit in the Supreme Court on October 26 regarding the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.
The ECI claims that the revision and its procedural alterations are within its constitutional remit and that decisions were unanimous.
Public facts and recorded objections by two Election Commissioners contradict the claim that the decisions were collective or unanimous.
The ECI stated that an additional declaration prescribed for Form 6 was a separate document rather than a rule amendment.
However, the ECI admitted online presentation could be construed as a Form 6 modification and that officer steps needed correction.
The ECI admitted the West Bengal CEO filed 1.6 million appeals before judicial tribunals but failed to answer who authorised them.
Failed attempts by Electoral Registration Officers in Goa to reverse voter deletions also remain unexplained in the affidavit.
The editorial urges the Supreme Court to test the affidavit's assertions using documents, file notings, and meeting minutes rather than accepting it at face value.
sum.text:
<p>The Election Commission of India (ECI)’s affidavit filed in the Supreme Court on October 26 raises more questions than it answers about the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the functioning of the Commission. </p>.<p>While it maintains that the SIR and its procedural alterations are within the ECI’s constitutional remit and that the Commission’s decisions were unanimous, these claims are not borne out by the facts now public. The Commission cites honourable intentions, but intent must be supported by practice and procedure.
</p>.<p>There is no dispute on the ECI’s constitutional powers, but their exercise points to an unconstitutional intent. The affidavit notes that the objections recorded by two of the three Election Commissioners – Vivek Joshi and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu – were part of a consultative process. </p>.<p>It does not counter the point that most objections concerned decisions taken without keeping the two commissioners informed.
Given that these objections are on record, the decisions cannot be termed collective or unanimous.</p>.<p>In the affidavit, the ECI says the additional declaration it prescribed for Form 6 was a separate document, not a modification of the requirements under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. But it agrees that the way it appeared online “could be construed as though an amendment of Form 6 had been made” and that “certain steps taken by the officers” had “to be corrected”. </p>.<p>This position contradicts an earlier statement that the declaration was “upheld” by the Supreme Court and validates the charge of modification.
The additional document amounts to an amendment enforced by the Commission.</p>.RSS plans poll outreach; to focus on SIR in UP, drug abuse in Punjab.<p>Regarding West Bengal, the ECI admits that the state Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) filed 1.6 million appeals before judicial tribunals against the inclusion of voters. But it does not answer the question: Who authorised these appeals? Failed attempts by Electoral Registration Officers in Goa to reverse the deletion of some voters also remain unexplained.</p>.<p>The claims made in the affidavit need supporting evidence.
Some of them contradict available facts. The apex court should test the affidavit for the veracity of its assertions with documents, file notings, and minutes of the Commission’s meetings and consultations. It should…

The United States is consumed by its declining power. Iran has been a target for more than 70 years. In 1953, the CIA and British intelligence overthrew Iran’s elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh, after he nationalised Iran’s oil. The United States then installed the shah and backed his police state until the Iranian people overthrew it in 1979. The US has never forgiven Iran for escaping from US domination. The US backed Saddam Hussein’s deadly war against Iran in the 1980s, and followed with four decades of economic warfare, covert operations, cyberattacks and assassinations. Trump tore up the 2015 nuclear agreement in 2018, bombed Iran’s nuclear sites in June 2025, and then, in February of this year, joined Israel in open war, killing Iran’s supreme leader in the opening strikes.
Washington’s fixation on Iran is in the service of American hegemony. In The Grand Chessboard (1997), Zbigniew Brzezinski named Iran one of five “geopolitical pivots,” states that matter less for their own power than for where they sit. Iran commands the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. Brzezinski wrote that an “antihegemonic” coalition of China, Russia and Iran could emerge “only if the United States is shortsighted enough to antagonize China and Iran simultaneously.” Well, yes, Washington has been that shortsighted and reckless.
The signs that the war will restart are not hidden. This week, War Secretary Pete Hegseth visited Israel to discuss renewed joint strikes, and Israeli sources report that the plans target Iran’s petrochemical facilities and nuclear sites. The White House has promised that the United States will not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections, which is another way of announcing a timetable for war. The US naval blockade of Iran’s ports has passed its 100th day. Trump rejected Iran’s proposal for a seven-day ceasefire in September, even though Tehran says the offer remains on the table.
Israel’s October 27 election adds fuel to the fire. On October 18, Trump endorsed Netanyahu , saying the United States would “finish the job” against Iran only with Netanyahu in charge. On October 21, at a rally in Dimona (home to the reactor where Israel secretly built its own nuclear arsenal), Netanyahu declared that the only way to end the Iranian threat is to overthrow the regime and said he had issued that directive to the army, Mossad and the security services.

points: Implementation of the Four-Year Undergraduate Programme in Delhi University faces severe imbroglios, notably leaving fourth-year pass-outs stranded regarding one-year postgraduate programme admissions.
Unclear priority parameters and last-minute rule changes have driven affected students to approach courts seeking legal relief against admission denials.
The core issue stems from policy confusion, poor infrastructure, and guidelines formulated after programmes commence, leaving students and teachers insecure and clueless.
The current National Education Policy 2020 and FYUP trace their commercial and market-aligned roots back to the 2000 Ambani-Birla report and earlier FYUP iterations.
Higher education faces inherent contradictions between aligning with market demands and introducing extraneous ideological burdens and peripheral courses like Value Addition Courses.
About 45 percent of scores depend on internal assessments, leading to a scramble for credits without meaningful effort and diluting core disciplinary depth.
Overloading the curriculum with peripheral courses erodes genuine learning and critical thinking, adding little real value to the additional fourth year of study.
The author concludes that current training turns students into efficient consumers of knowledge rather than nurturing independent, critical thinkers.
sum.text:
This newspaper recently reported (‘The Fourth-Year Trap’, IE , October 26) on yet another imbroglio involving the implementation of FYUP (Four-Year Undergraduate Programme) in the University of Delhi, centred this time on the problems faced by those fourth-year pass-outs who thought they had a last-minute ticket to the one-year PG programme, but were turned away at the boarding gate. That ticket was part of the hard sell that has surrounded FYUP, which has included a slew of offers and incentives to make it work. Hard-selling without the inventory to back up what’s being offered results in irate customers. Many students who have been denied admission to the one-year PG course based on priority parameters set by the university have moved the courts seeking relief.
The FYUP problem is entangled with the larger story around the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020. Regardless of whether NEP has merit or otherwise (it works very well for engineering colleges, for example), its implementation across India’s universities has experienced roadblocks; continual attempts at steadying the project have led to further complications. Guidelines and rules are often formulated after programmes are started; unclear rules of engagement leave teachers and students clueless about requirements and entitlements, frequent changes and exacting requirements in the face of weak infrastructure result in cutting corners to meet timelines, and most disturbingly, students are insecure in the absence of clarity.
At the heart of the problem is the big picture, which, to my mind, is not as big as it is made out to be. To blame the university and its officials is to shrink the problem into visible targets. Moreover, the problem is “secular”, as it were. It begins with the Ambani-Birla report, the Report on a Policy Framework for Reforms in Education, submitted in 2000, and readily championed by Congress after it came to power in 2004 (recall FYUP version 1.0 under then HRD minister Kapil Sibal). It hinged on commerce (privatisation and corporatisation, higher student fees, and so on, which this piece will not dwell on), positing that education ought not to be thought of as something that exists apart from the commercial interests of society. It also suggested, perhaps even more troublingly, that higher education should align strictly with skills, be depoliticised and attend supinely to the exigencies of the knowledge economy. Many critics have argued that the older policy has segued into…

points: The Inter-State Council is a mechanism conceived to promote cooperative federalism in India, but it has largely remained dormant due to infrequent meetings and operational limitations.
The Inter-State Council Secretariat was set up in 1991 and has also functioned as the secretariat for Zonal Councils since 2011.
Zonal Councils are statutory bodies established under Part III of the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 to handle regional issues.
There are five Zonal Councils covering the North, South, East, West, and Central regions, chaired by the Union Home Minister.
The North Eastern Council was created under the North Eastern Council Act of 1972 to address unique regional development challenges.
The Inter-State Council serves to promote cooperative federalism, provide structured dialogue, build consensus, and investigate inter-State disputes under Article 263.
Key limitations of the Inter-State Council include infrequent meetings, its purely advisory nature, and the Centre's dominance in agenda setting.
Political dynamics and adversarial atmospheres between the Centre and States further hinder collaborative problem-solving within the Council.
sum.text:
The Council is assisted by a secretariat called the Inter-State Council Secretariat . This secretariat was set-up in 1991 and is headed by a secretary to the Government of India. Since 2011, it is also functioning as the secretariat of the Zonal Councils.
Zonal Councils are Statutory Bodies . They were established under Part III of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 .
Zonal Councils are the regional counterparts to the national-level ISC. They were created to address issues specific to different regions of the country.
There are 5 Zonal Councils , each covering a specific geographical region of India – North, South, East, West & Central Zonal Councils.
Composition: Common Chairman : The Union Home Minister chairs all five Zonal Councils. Vice-Chairman : The Chief Ministers of the States in the zone act as Vice-Chairman by rotation, usually for one year. Advisors : One person nominated by the NITI Aayog and the Chief Secretaries of each State (they participate but cannot vote).

The application for bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid was filed by the US-based non-profit Global Alliance for TB Drug Development.
BPaL is an all-oral WHO-recommended regimen replacing older treatments that lasted over a year and involved painful daily injections.
India's national TB programme uses BPaLM, adding moxifloxacin, and has started it for more than 15,000 patients.
The rejection followed pre-grant oppositions filed in 2020 by activists, TB survivors, and public health groups.

sum.text:
The Indian Patent Office on Tuesday rejected a patent application for BPaL, a combination of three medicines that has cut treatment for drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) to six months, according to a joint statement by the groups that opposed it.
The application, for the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid, was filed by the Global Alliance for TB Drug Development (TB Alliance), a US-based non-profit that developed pretomanid.
TB Alliance did not respond to HT’s requests for comment till the time of going to print.
BPaL is an all-oral regimen recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) for eligible patients with drug-resistant TB. It replaces older regimens that could run for more than a year and often involved painful daily injections. Under India’s national TB programme, more than 15,000 patients have started BPaLM, the same regimen with a fourth drug, moxifloxacin, added.
The rejection followed two pre-grant oppositions filed in 2020. Indian patent law allows anyone to challenge a patent application before it is granted. One was filed by Eldred Tellis of the Sankalp Rehabilitation Trust and Ganesh Acharya, a two-time TB survivor, with support from the Lawyers Collective and Médecins Sans Frontières’ Access Campaign. The other was filed by the Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+), with support from Third World Network (TWN).
“The opponents challenged the patent application on the grounds that the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid, as well as its use in a shorter treatment regimen, had already been disclosed in earlier scientific research and clinical trials dating back to 2015,” the joint statement said. They argued that combining known medicines did not amount to an inventive step that justified a new patent.
In 2023, the patent office had rejected an application by Johnson & Johnson to extend its patent on bedaquiline.
The opponents said the decision could help open the door to generic competition and lower prices in India and elsewhere. Patents on the BPaL combination have been granted in 11 countries and are due to expire in 2036: Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Bulgaria, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, South Africa, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.
India had an estimated 2.71 million new TB cases in 2024, about a quarter of the global total, or 187 for every 100,000 people, according to WHO.

It also questioned how electoral entries could be reopened on the basis of patterns identified through the revision exercise, and whether the process involved meaningful human scrutiny.

The ECI is tasked with maintaining accurate electoral rolls, removing ineligible entries and ensuring that eligible citizens are registered. But the court’s questions centre on how far the commission can go in flagging existing voters for verification, what standards it uses and whether its methodology is legally sustainable.

sum.text:
The Union Cabinet has approved the Pradhan Mantri Viksit Gram Swaraj Yojana (PM VGSY), a Centrally Sponsored Scheme aimed at strengthening village-level governance, improving development planning and making Panchayats more financially accountable.
The scheme will run from 2026-27 to 2030-31, in line with the tenure of the Sixteenth Finance Commission. It has a total outlay of ₹ 7,395.55 crore, comprising a central share of ₹ 4,869.48 crore and a state share of ₹ 2,526.07 crore, according to the Press Information Bureau (PIB) release dated 28 October 2026.
The initiative is expected to directly benefit around 32 lakh elected representatives, Panchayat functionaries and other stakeholders across more than 2.55 lakh Panchayats and traditional local bodies. The government also aims to reach at least one crore citizens through each coordinated public awareness exercise.
A key objective of PM VGSY is to improve coordination between central ministries, state governments and local bodies so that village development plans reflect local priorities and make better use of available funds.

sum.text:
Washington, Oct 29 (PTI) The IMF on Thursday said the impact of weather events such as the Super El Nino was yet to materialise for India, which remains the engine of growth for the world economy.
The IMF listed lower crop yields, increased food price inflation and its impact on the purchasing power of households in India due to the Super El Nino.
“So these are risks that we see that India faces, but right now those risks have not materialised,” IMF Communications Director Julie Kozack told a press conference here.
She said the IMF will reassess India's growth projections in the January World Economic Outlook update after the risks posed by the weather event materialise.
Earlier this month, the IMF raised India’s growth forecast for fiscal year 2027 and fiscal year 2028 to 7 per cent, from the 6.4 per cent and 6.7 per cent projections respectively made in July.
“So, we see it really as a risk going forward, and of course depending on whether that risk materialises, we will reassess our growth projections for India the next time in our January WEO update,” Kozack said.
“But for now what we see is quite strong growth momentum in India, and it continues to be an engine of growth,” the IMF official said.
Kozack said the 7 per cent growth projection for FY-27 and FY-28 in the IMF’s World Economic Outlook report released in Bangkok earlier this month was supported by robust domestic demand and strong services activity in India. PTI SKU ZH

points: The Commission for Air Quality Management invoked Stage I of the Graded Response Action Plan as Delhi's Air Quality Index entered the Poor category.
GRAP is a set of short-term emergency measures designed to reduce air pollution when air quality deteriorates in Delhi and NCR districts.
First notified by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change in January 2017, GRAP operates through four increasingly stringent stages.
State governments implement the measures through respective orders and are legally bound to comply with directions from the Commission.
The Commission for Air Quality Management replaced the Environment Pollution Prevention and Control Authority in 2021 to ensure better enforcement.
Under Stage III, restrictions apply to BS-III petrol and BS-IV or older diesel light motor vehicles, while Stage IV restricts construction and truck entry.
Winter pollution in Delhi-NCR is driven by low wind speeds, vehicular emissions, construction dust, stubble burning, and festive-season firecrackers.
An analysis by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air found no consistent improvement in winter air quality over four years.
The Delhi government also introduced seasonal vehicle bans and doubled parking charges from November to February to curb emissions.
sum.text:
Graded Response Action Plan Latest News The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) invoked Stage I of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) as Delhi’s Air Quality Index (AQI) entered the ‘Poor’ category, renewing debate over the effectiveness of emergency pollution-control measures. Understanding the Graded Response Action Plan The Graded Response Action Plan is a set of short-term emergency measures designed to reduce air pollution when air quality deteriorates. First notified by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change in January 2017, it was introduced following Supreme Court directions.
GRAP operates through four stages, with increasingly stringent restrictions corresponding to worsening air quality. The CAQM announces the applicable stages based on recorded pollution levels or forecasts. Its directions cover Delhi and the National Capital Region (NCR) districts of Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan.
State governments implement the measures through their respective orders and are legally bound to comply with CAQM directions. Institutional Evolution Initially, GRAP was implemented by the Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority (EPCA), established in 1998. However, concerns about its limited statutory powers weakened its ability to enforce compliance.
In 2021, the Commission for Air Quality Management replaced the EPCA and assumed responsibility for implementing GRAP. The plan has since undergone multiple revisions to strengthen pollution-control measures. Four Stages of GRAP The restrictions become progressively more stringent as Delhi’s AQI rises.
Under Stage III, restrictions apply to BS-III petrol and BS-IV or older diesel light motor vehicles in Delhi and specified high-vehicle-density districts. Stage IV further restricts construction activities and truck entry, with exemptions for specified cleaner-fuel and BS-VI vehicles. Although GRAP can be imposed throughout the year, its higher stages are predominantly activated during winter, when meteorological conditions worsen pollution.
Factors Behind Delhi-NCR’s Winter Pollution Winter air pollution results from a combination of emissions and atmospheric conditions. Meteorological conditions: Lower wind speeds and falling temperatures hinder the dispersion of pollutants. Vehicular emissions: Road transport contributes to the concentration of pollutants in the region.
Construction and road dust: Dust-generating activities add particulate matter to the atmosphere.…

sum.text:
MUMBAI: The Indian economy is estimated to grow by 7.35 per cent in the July-September quarter supported by strong domestic demand, industrial activity and higher consumption, as against 7.8 per cent growth seen in April-June, the Ministry of Finance said in its Monthly Economic Review for October released on Thursday. The ministry said that the focus of policymakers during the second half of the financial year will be “sustaining economic activity while safeguarding price stability” amidst elevated crude oil prices, higher food inflation and an uncertain outlook for the kharif crop. The review cited a host of high frequency indicators such as GST collections, E-way bill generation, freight and logistics indicators, petrol and diesel consumption, automobile sales that point to sustained domestic demand and continued economic momentum in Q2 FY27, consistent with the improved growth outlook.
Reflecting these favourable conditions, bank credit growth remained strong at 21.6 per cent year-on-year as of September 30. The business activity moderated in Q2, but showed signs of strengthening towards the end of the quarter. The recovery in PMI readings, alongside improved business sentiment, points to a cautiously favourable outlook for the coming months.
Healthy credit growth and recent trade agreements are expected to provide additional support to consumption, investment and exports. “Taken together, these indicators point to sustained growth momentum in Q2 FY27. Following real GDP growth of 7.8 per cent in Q1 FY27, the Department’s nowcasting model, introduced in the Economic Survey 2025-26, nowcasts real GDP growth of 7.35 per cent in Q2 FY27,” the review said.
On inflation, the report said that near-term dynamics will be shaped by a combination of domestic food supply management, global energy volatility, and systemic liquidity conditions. On the food front, supply-side interventions such as Kharif onion releases via the ‘Kanda Express’, stockholding limits on sugar dealers, and Basic Customs Duty (BCD) cuts on crude edible oils are expected to ease price pressures on key kitchen staples. However, downside risks persist from an intensifying El Niño event that threatens soil moisture during the upcoming Rabi sowing season, as well as demand-side pressure during the festive period.
Externally, elevated crude oil prices and maritime freight disruptions across the West Asian transit routes pose ongoing upside risks to input costs, though recent RBI measures to…

points: The Supreme Court struck down the Karnataka Civil Services (Validation of Selection and Appointment of 2011 Batch Gazetted Probationers) Act, 2022 as unconstitutional.
A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran ruled that the legislature cannot override judicial decisions upholding the cancellation of a tainted recruitment.
The core issue involved the legislature attempting to validate appointments made through a 2011 recruitment process marred by widespread corruption and nepotism.
The 2011 notification aimed to fill 362 posts, for which 1,38,307 candidates applied and 1,090 were eventually called for interviews.
A CID investigation revealed serious manipulation, including call records linking candidates with KPSC members, identical interview marks, and evidence destruction.
The Karnataka government previously cancelled the selection, and this cancellation was upheld earlier by both the Karnataka High Court and the Supreme Court.
Despite the judicial setbacks, Karnataka enacted the 2022 validation law citing hardship for candidates not directly accused of individual wrongdoing.

sum.text:
The Supreme Court on Thursday struck down as unconstitutional a Karnataka law that validated appointments made through the state's tainted 2011 recruitment of gazetted probationers, news agency Press Trust of India reported. A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran held that the legislature could not override judicial decisions that had upheld the cancellation of a recruitment process marred by widespread corruption and nepotism. The court allowed appeals challenging the Karnataka Civil Services (Validation of Selection and Appointment of 2011 Batch Gazetted Probationers) Act, 2022.
Appointments had been made under the law despite earlier findings of serious irregularities in the selection process."We have no doubt in our minds that the subject legislation is unconstitutional. We set aside the same, as also the judgments impugned herein, both in the PIL and the writ petition filed against the order of the KAT (Karnataka Administrative Tribunal). The PIL, though not agitated by the individual who filed it, would stand allowed, transposing the appellants herein as the petitioners," the judgment said.
The Supreme Court directed the Karnataka government to begin fresh recruitment for the vacancies remaining in Group A and Group B services under the existing rules. It also ordered a one-time relaxation of the age limit for specified categories of candidates. These include the six appellants, eligible candidates from the earlier selection process and petitioners in pending proceedings before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal."Having found the Act of 2022 unconstitutional, we cannot but observe that the appointments made pursuant to the tainted recruitment will also come to an end.
The passage of a decade and a half from the initial recruitment restrains us from resuming the entire selection from the stage at which it was found tainted; i.e., after the stage of the preliminary examination," the court said. The bench directed the state government to issue a fresh recruitment notification for the vacant posts."Insofar as the persons who are continuing now, if selected, their seniority shall also be only from the date of their fresh appointment as per the selection and recruitment directed by us. However, if the persons working now get selected and appointed, the period they have been in service pursuant to their earlier appointment shall be reckoned for computation of their pension and retirement benefits," it…

sum.text:
The European Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee Chair, David McAllister, has said that the India-EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA) is expected to be signed by mid-December 2026, with PM Narendra Modi anticipated to travel to Brussels for the official signing ceremony. The "mother of all deals" will still undergo rigorous scrutiny by the European Parliament, but McAllister told TOI in an interview he's confident about smooth ratification, given the benefits it will bring to both sides. The EU lawmaker said that a consent vote is expected by spring next year, paving the way for the trade agreement to officially enter into force mid-2027." We expect the FTA to be signed by mid-December.
Hopefully, PM Modi will manage to visit Brussels and attend the official signing ceremony," said McAllister, who led an EU Parliamentary delegation to India this week." Though Parliament cannot amend the text of the agreement, our consent is required before it enters into force. I followed the debate in the European Parliament over the past months, and I can say there seems to be a broad majority support for this landmark FTA. The benefits for both sides are so huge that I'm sure the European Parliament will give its support in the consent vote," added McAllister, who heads the Parliamentary committee that shapes and monitors the EU's common foreign and security policy.
McAllister also said the EU would particularly welcome progress on the investment protection agreement as it would strengthen the confidence of European investors in the Indian market, encouraging greater European investments and contributing to job creation in India. He said the FTA would allow India and the EU to work more closely on de-risking supply chains and reducing dependencies. If the FTA indeed is ready for signing by mid-December, Modi is likely to stop over in Brussels to ink the deal on his way back to India from the US G20 summit.
The PM will also travel to Canada and possibly to Germany during that trip. Asked about the prospects of defence-industrial collaboration and technology sharing under the new India-EU defence and security partnership, McAllister backed closer cooperation between India and the European defence industry, saying it is in the interest of both sides. sum.text:
The Rajya Sabha on Monday passed the Bankers’ Books Evidence Bill, 2026, paving the way for replacing the colonial-era Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 1891, with a modern legal framework aligned with the country’s increasingly digital banking system.
The Lok Sabha had already passed the Bill on August 5. With its passage by both Houses of Parliament, the legislation seeks to update the legal framework governing the use of bankers’ books and records as evidence in judicial proceedings.
The Bill retains most of the provisions of the existing law, under which certified copies of bank records can be produced as evidence in legal proceedings without requiring the original records.
A key provision of the new legislation is the explicit recognition of electronic and digital records of bankers’ books as admissible, valid and legally enforceable evidence, subject to specified safeguards.
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the Bill provides for a technology-neutral legal framework for bankers’ books and recognises electronic and digital banking records.
Under the proposed framework, an electronic or digital copy would be admissible if it is a true copy of the relevant entry or information and accurately represents or is appropriately derived from the original record.
The Bill also requires safeguards to ensure the integrity of electronic records. No unauthorised alteration of data should have occurred, while there should be no tampering with the system or any other event that could undermine the integrity and accuracy of the record.
Under the existing framework, a bank officer cannot ordinarily be compelled to produce a banker’s book in a proceeding to which the bank is not a party, or to appear as a witness to prove matters, transactions or accounts recorded in such books. However, a court or judge may order such production or appearance for a special cause.
The 2026 Bill specifies circumstances that may constitute such a special cause. These include situations where the accuracy or genuineness of an entry or information is in doubt, where an event indicates an interruption in the regular process of maintaining records, or where a bank fails to comply with a court order relating to inspection of its books.
Sitharaman said the legislation would also strengthen statutory protection available to bank officers when the bank is not a party to the proceedings.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday said that delay in execution of arbitral awards strikes at the very rationale of adopting arbitration over conventional litigation and asked the Law Commission of India to make legislative and procedural recommendations to strengthen the execution regime. A bench headed by justice Vikram Nath said, “The efficacy of an arbitral regime cannot be measured merely by the expedition with which an award is rendered or the circumscribed grounds upon which it may be challenged. It must equally be assessed by the ability of the successful party to realise the fruits of the award within a reasonable time.” The court was deciding an appeal filed by Royal Construction Company Pvt.
which had won an award against National Projects Construction Corporation Ltd. (NPCC) in 2002 and was awaiting its execution for the past 24 years. The bench, also comprising justices Sandeep Mehta and Aparesh Kumar Singh said, “More than 24 years after the arbitral award was rendered, the parties continue to litigate over its enforcement.
Such a state of affairs strikes at the very rationale underlying the adoption of arbitration as an effective alternative to conventional civil litigation.” The court said that the present case was not a solitary instance as the experience of similar cases calls for a closer examination of whether this framework under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 has adequately served the objectives it was meant to achieve.“The promise of arbitration remains unfulfilled if a party, having traversed the arbitral process, is compelled to embark upon another protracted course of litigation to secure the benefit of the award,” the court said, as it entrusted the Law Commission to make “such legislative or procedural recommendations” necessary to ensure that the enforcement of arbitral awards is commensurate with the objectives of the 1996 Act and India’s commitment to establishing itself as an arbitration-friendly jurisdiction.“In these circumstances, we request the Law Commission of India to undertake a focused study of the statutory and procedural framework governing the enforcement and execution of arbitral awards,” the judgment said. sum.text:
The government has announced higher Minimum Support Prices (MSP) for six mandated Rabi crops for the 2027–28 marketing season, providing farmers with increased price support for the upcoming agricultural cycle. The revised rates are intended to help farmers receive better returns and encourage crop diversification.
Under the revised structure, the highest increase is for safflower, while rapeseed and mustard and lentils have also received substantial hikes.
The approved MSP rates for the 2027–28 marketing season are:
Safflower has received the largest increase of ₹675 per quintal compared with the previous marketing season. Rapeseed and mustard follow with a rise of ₹413, while lentil prices have increased by ₹390 per quintal.
The government estimates that approximately ₹90,962 crore will be paid to farmers for around 324 lakh metric tonnes of produce during the Rabi Marketing Season 2027–28.
MSP is designed to provide a measure of price assurance to farmers and support decisions about crop selection and agricultural investment. Actual procurement and payments depend on the applicable procurement arrangements and eligibility requirements.
The MSP system aims to protect farmers from sharp market-price fluctuations by announcing minimum support prices for specified crops. The government also considers production costs, including inputs, equipment depreciation, working-capital interest and family labour, when calculating MSP.
The latest rates maintain the policy of setting MSP at least 50% above the estimated cost of production across the mandated crops, according to the government’s published figures.
Farmers planning their Rabi crop cycle can use the revised MSP figures as one factor when making cultivation decisions. However, an announced MSP does not automatically mean that every farmer will sell all produce at that price.
Farmers should check procurement arrangements, registration requirements and local purchasing details with the relevant authorities before relying on MSP procurement for their expected income.

The matter has been listed for further hearing on November 17 along with pending petitions.
At the outset, senior advocate Madhavi Divan, appearing for the DNPA, urged the bench to consider the stay application, saying that the absence of an exemption for journalistic activities could fundamentally change how news is gathered and reported.
"This is perhaps the first comprehensive petition by what we call legacy media. There has been some debate over citizen journalists. We are the traditional, conventional legacy media," she said.
The senior lawyer said requiring journalists to seek permission from individuals before publishing information about them could undermine the functioning of newsrooms.
She also raised concerns about the amendment to Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information (RTI) Act, which deals with the disclosure of personal information held by public authorities.
The absence of a journalistic exemption amounts to pre-censorship of the press and could have serious consequences for news coverage, she said.
"We have raised the argument concerning exemptions as well. Otherwise, newsrooms will shut down if we have to ask for permission.

Divan said earlier laws had excluded journalism and questioned why the exemption had not been retained.
"When the court examines this Act in detail, it will find that it was not meant for journalism at all. In fact, the earlier versions excluded journalism. We do not know why this has happened. Clearly, it was not meant for us," she said.

static: Section 31 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) governs the sentencing of a person for multiple offences at one trial.
Section 31(1) permits a court to direct sentences of imprisonment to run consecutively, but excludes imprisonment for life from this provision.

explain.video_query: Supreme Court multiple life sentences consecutive superimposition

points: The Supreme Court ruled that life sentences awarded for multiple offences in a single trial cannot run consecutively.
The trigger was a special leave petition filed by Raju Shantaram Koli challenging consecutive life sentences.
The core issue is that directing humans to undergo life imprisonment twice is irrational because a person has only one life.
A bench of Justices K V Vishwanathan and Arun Palli partly allowed the petition against the Bombay High Court order.
The appellant was convicted for offences committed on April 29, 2010, including rape and murder of a 12-year-old girl.
The trial court on September 27, 2013, and the Bombay High Court on June 10, 2016, had ordered consecutive life sentences.
The apex court relied on the Constitution bench ruling in Muthuramalingam vs State (2016) to declare multiple life sentences must superimpose.
Superimposition ensures that remission or commutation granted for one life sentence does not automatically extend to the other.
sum.text:
<p>New Delhi: The Supreme Court on Tuesday underlined that life sentences awarded for multiple offences in a single trial cannot be directed to run consecutively, and must instead be superimposed so that remission or commutation granted for one does not automatically extend to the other.</p><p>A bench of Justices K V Vishwanathan and Arun Palli reiterated the legal position while partly allowing a special leave petition filed by Raju Shantaram Koli. </p><p>The Bombay High Court had on June 10, 2016, upheld a trial court judgment of September 27, 2013, which directed the appellant to undergo consecutive life sentences for the rape and murder of a 12-year-old girl.</p><p>Koli was arrested on April 30, 2010, for the offences committed on April 29, 2010, under Sections 302 and 376 read with Section 342 of the Indian Penal Code. Both the trial court and the High Court had ordered the life sentences to run one after the other.</p>.'Free sale of acid defeats orders': Supreme Court tells Centre to file compliance report.<p>The apex court referred to the Constitution bench ruling in Muthuramalingam and Others vs State (2016), which held that directing an offender to undergo imprisonment for life twice over would be anomalous and irrational, as humans have only one life to live. </p><p>Section 31(1) of the CrPC permits consecutive sentences only if they are not life sentences.
Multiple life sentences, the Constitution bench said, would get superimposed over each other, ensuring that remission or commutation of one does not ipso facto result in remission of the other.</p><p>Applying this principle, the bench set aside the High Court order to the extent it upheld consecutive running of the two life sentences. It declared that the life sentence under Section 302 and the life sentence under Section 376 read with Section 342 would stand superimposed over each other. The remaining part of the High Court judgment was upheld.</p><p>The court condoned the delay, admitted the special leave petition, and noted that it was not required to examine the related writ petition, which raised a question whether a writ court could order concurrent sentences.</p>

sum.text:
New Delhi [India], October 29: The 19th Meeting of the Ganga Flood Control Board (GFCB) was held at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, on Thursday under the chairmanship of Union Minister of Jal Shakti, C R Patil. The meeting was also attended by West Bengal Chief Minister, Suvendu Adhikari. According to the Union Ministry of Jal Shakti, the meeting reviewed ongoing initiatives, strengthened interstate coordination and deliberated on emerging approaches for effective flood management.
During the meeting, the Jal Shakti Minister launched the Punah Bharan Mobile App, developed by the Bhaskaracharya National Institute for Space Applications and Geo-informatics in collaboration with the National Water Mission.&nbsp; The application aims to facilitate scientific identification of suitable locations for artificial groundwater recharge interventions. Sibal argued that under the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, the state government has the power to refer any case to the CBI.

sum.text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in New Delhi on Friday to attend the 18th BRICS Summit and is scheduled to hold bilateral talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi later in the day.
Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal welcomed the Russian President in a post on X.
“Warmly welcome President Vladimir Putin of Russia for the 18th BRICS Summit. He was received by MoS @KVSinghMPGonda at the airport. India and Russia share multifaceted and longstanding ties anchored in Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership,” Jaiswal said.
Putin was received at the airport by Minister of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh.
The Russian President’s visit comes amid continued high-level engagement between New Delhi and Moscow and follows his meeting with PM Modi on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Bishkek last week.
During their meeting in Bishkek, PM Modi had called for an end to the Russia-Ukraine conflict, saying the world needs to move from an “endless war” towards the “end of war”.
“We have to move from a situation of ‘endless war’ to ‘end of war’… It is humanity’s wish that the end of this war happens as soon as possible,” PM Modi had said.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, speaking to Indian media persons ahead of Putin’s visit, had said the two leaders would discuss bilateral relations as well as ongoing international issues. He also indicated that Putin would brief PM Modi on the latest developments concerning the Ukraine conflict.
India, as BRICS Chair for 2026, is hosting the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12-13. The summit will bring together leaders of BRICS member and partner countries as well as Outreach Invitees.
According to the MEA, leaders at the summit will exchange views on strengthening intra-BRICS cooperation on common priorities and share perspectives on global and regional issues of mutual importance.
Putin’s arrival in New Delhi marks an important engagement between the two countries as India prepares to host the high-level BRICS gathering, with his meeting with PM Modi expected to further shape discussions on bilateral, regional and international issues.

points: Tripura Chief Minister Manik Saha and power minister Ratan Lal Nath laid the foundation stone for an underground cabling project under the Agartala Smart Grid initiative.
They also launched the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana under the Utility-Led Aggregation (ULA) model in the state.
The initiatives aim to upgrade power infrastructure in Agartala and offer assistance to low-income households.
The underground cabling project is estimated to cost Rs 1,151 crore and will replace overhead power lines across a wider area of Agartala.
Funding for the cabling project includes Rs 131 crore from the state government, Rs 495 crore from the Centre, and a Rs 525-crore loan from the Asian Development Bank (ADB).
Under the solar power scheme, the government plans to cover 1.5 lakh households in the first phase within six months.

sum.text:
Agartala: Tripura chief minister Manik Saha and power minister Ratan Lal Nath on Thursday laid the foundation stone for the underground cabling project as part of the Agartala Smart Grid initiative and launched the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana under the Utility-Led Aggregation (ULA) model. Nath said these initiatives aim to upgrade the power infrastructure in Agartala and offer assistance to low-income households. The underground cabling project, estimated to cost Rs 1,151 crore, will replace overhead power lines across a wider area of Agartala.
Its funding includes Rs 131 crore from the state govt, Rs 495 crore from the Centre and a Rs 525-crore loan from Asian Development Bank (ADB). Under the solar power scheme, govt plans to cover 1.5 lakh households in the first phase. The goal is to enrol these households in the scheme within six months.
Eligible beneficiaries will pay Rs 1,000 as a security deposit, while govt will manage the installation and recover this amount as a security deposit. The solar systems are expected to reduce electricity bills, particularly for low-income households with monthly consumption of around 50 units.
